papers.title: Understanding the Inner Workings of a State-Space Foundation Model for Limit Order Books
papers.abstract: Autoregressive foundation models offer state-of-the-art capabilities to simulate the market by generating the message flow of limit order books (LOBs). Yet, without understanding their inner workings, research directions are hard to narrow and practical use in real-world trading environments remains uncertain. This study therefore asks what these models actually learn about market microstructure. We find that, similarly to games where sequence models build an internal representation of the board, an 8.2M-parameter Mamba-3 state-space model trained autoregressively on the tokenized message stream of eight large-cap US equities learns an internal representation of the market and its dynamics. In particular, order-flow imbalance, a central driver of short-horizon price moves, is decodable at $R^2 \approx 0.59$, far above controls and baselines. This representation extends to unseen stocks, suggesting that these models learn general representations rather than ticker-specific patterns. The model also generalizes across metrics beyond order-flow imbalance: results hold across traded volume and volatility. Additionally, the representation is causally steerable: pushing the state along a feature's axis shifts the model's next-message beliefs as that feature implies, monotonically in dose, consistent with the emergence of a world model.

papers.title: Strategic Index Reconstitution: Differential Games, Closed-Loop Equilibria and Mean-Field Dynamics
papers.abstract: We study a continuous-time, multiasset trading game around index reconstitution, in which opportunistic traders have heterogeneous beliefs about the future index constitution and interact through transient cross-asset price impact and instantaneous execution costs. Opportunistic traders build inventory based on their individual beliefs about the future index constitution before a public announcement, adjust their positions to the revealed composition, and unwind them against the indexer's prescribed rebalancing trades at the implementation date when the new index composition takes effect. Under a no-price-manipulation condition, we construct a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. Its affine feedback policies are computed from a non-standard matrix Riccati equation and linear ODEs whose number and dimensions are independent of population size. Under mean-field scaling, we construct a mean-field equilibrium and obtain quantitative convergence and approximate-Nash bounds. Numerical illustrations show that greater competition among opportunists dampens price swings around implementation and that opportunistic trading lowers the indexer's implementation shortfall unless price resilience is very low. Holding the average belief fixed, greater belief dispersion can increase gross trading volume without changing net aggregate opportunist holdings or price impact.

papers.title: Combinatorial Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
papers.abstract: We develop a framework to identify and quantify arbitrage across logically related prediction-market contracts. We prove that prices outside the convex hull of admissible payoff vectors admit arbitrage and identify optimal arbitrage portfolios through integer programming. Using venue metadata and semantic analysis of resolution criteria, we recover 1.9 million logical relations and compile them into constraint systems covering more than 255,000 contracts. We replay full-depth Polymarket order books to simulate an arbitrageur executing these portfolios against resting orders. Among settled portfolios, an ideal arbitrageur that takes the full displayed depth of every opportunity and reuses its capital at resolution earns a risk-free return of 3.5% a week after spreads and fees. We find that arbitrage opportunities persist longer and attract less observed participation where relation discovery and execution are more costly.
